grades.A: Proven — running in real towns and cities
grades.B: Piloted — working plants, not yet common
grades.C: Lab stage — promising research, no utility runs it yet

items.name: Find the water you’re losing
items.what: Smart meters plus listening devices on the pipes find leaks early. Every gallon lost was already pumped and treated.
items.example: Hot Springs, Arkansas cut water it couldn’t account for from 44% to 24%, and found one broken valve wasting about 4 million gallons a day (the meter company’s case study).
items.limit: The case study comes from the company that sold the system. Savings depend on how leaky the pipes are to begin with.

items.name: Let bacteria clean it first (biological filtration)
items.what: A living layer on the sand or carbon filter eats organic matter and ammonia — with fewer chemicals. Less organic matter means fewer chlorine byproducts later. Slow sand filters work this way.
items.example: Slow sand filters have run for more than 150 years; several U.S. utilities have converted filters to biological operation.
items.limit: It doesn’t remove “forever chemicals” (PFAS) by itself, and slow sand filters need land.

items.name: Disinfect with UV light
items.what: Ultraviolet light kills germs without adding a chemical, so less chlorine is needed. Adding hydrogen peroxide under UV (advanced oxidation) breaks down trace chemicals too.
items.limit: Some chlorine is still needed to keep water safe inside the pipes.

items.name: Let the riverbank filter it
items.what: Wells beside a river pull water through natural sand and gravel, which filters it before it reaches the plant.
items.example: Louisville Water in Kentucky uses riverbank filtration.
items.limit: Only works where the ground next to the river is the right kind of sand and gravel — that takes a study.

items.name: Membranes (ultrafiltration)
items.what: Very fine filters physically block germs and particles. Packaged systems are sold for small towns.
items.limit: Membranes need cleaning and replacing, and they use electricity.

items.name: Remove “forever chemicals” (PFAS)
items.what: Activated carbon, ion exchange, and reverse osmosis remove PFAS. Destroying PFAS completely (supercritical water, electrochemical methods) is still in pilots.
items.limit: EPA set PFAS limits in 2024. In 2026 it proposed pushing the main deadline from 2029 to 2031 and dropping limits for four of the six chemicals — both still proposals. Test first, then decide.

items.name: Protect the source
items.what: Keeping the watershed healthy — forests, stream banks, fixing upstream sewage — is usually cheaper than treating dirty water.
items.example: New York City protected its Catskill watershed instead of building a filtration plant estimated at up to $10 billion.
items.limit: New York’s dollars don’t scale down; the idea does.

items.name: Constructed wetlands
items.what: Planted, shallow basins where plants, soil, and microbes clean treated wastewater further.
items.example: EPA guidance calls them well suited to small towns “where inexpensive land is available.”

src.label: Univ. of Arizona, summarizing EPA guidance

items.limit: Needs land, and works slower in cold weather.

items.name: Algae on moving belts
items.what: Algae grow on belts that rotate through lagoon water, pulling out phosphorus and nitrogen. The harvested algae can become fertilizer.
items.example: Gross-Wen Technologies (Iowa) — at least eight systems running in Iowa and Illinois.
items.limit: Still young, and algae slow down in winter.

items.name: Duckweed, fungi, and “living machines”
items.what: Floating plants, fungal filters, and greenhouse ecosystems that clean water. Duckweed pulled more than 93% of nitrogen and phosphorus from wastewater in a study.
items.limit: Strong study results, few full-size town plants to copy. Treat as a supplement, not a whole plant.

items.name: Recover energy and fertilizer
items.what: Digesting sludge makes biogas; phosphorus can be recovered as a fertilizer.
items.example: Tigard, Oregon became the first U.S. plant to recycle nutrients into commercial fertilizer (Ostara, 2009).
items.limit: Usually pays off only at bigger plants.

items.name: Metamaterials and solar evaporation
items.what: Engineered surfaces that soak up sunlight to evaporate and purify water.
items.limit: Researchers say fouling, cost, and scale still need to be solved. No utility runs it.

items.name: Graphene membranes
items.what: Ultra-thin carbon membranes that could filter faster with less energy.
items.limit: Research says most use is “still limited to laboratory scale.” No U.S. water utility uses them as its main filter yet.

ownership.text: Small towns aren’t alone: the National Rural Water Association and its state groups count over 31,000 member utility systems, and the Arkansas Rural Water Association is a nonprofit of rural and small publicly owned systems that trains and helps systems serving 10,000 people or fewer.

funding.text: State revolving funds lend water money that’s repaid into the same fund to lend again — part of some loans is forgiven.
USDA Rural Development lends and grants for water and sewer in rural areas and towns of 10,000 or fewer.
WIFIA offers low-cost federal loans for larger water projects.
